state.misconception_label: Assumes that an arrow on a number line starts at zero

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I have: ![Number line with -12 and -7 marked. Starting at -12, follow an arrow pointing to the right labelled +10. Then there is an arrow labelled b pointing to the left, which ends at -7 on the number line.]() What is the value of \( b \) ? I got \( -7 \) because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Imagine you're starting at a specific point on a road and you take a 10-mile drive to the right. If you then drive 5 miles back to the left, where would you end up? Think about how this relates to the number line and the direction of the arrows you're following.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I think I get what you're saying about the driving example. So if I start at -12 and go 10 to the right, I end up at -2, right? But then if I go back 5 to the left, I would be at -7. But I'm still confused about how that helps me find \( b \). Does \( b \) start from -12 or from somewhere else?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Imagine you're playing a game where you start at a specific point on a playground and take 10 steps to the right. After that, you take 5 steps back to the left. Where would you end up on the playground? Think about how this relates to the number line and the direction of the arrows you're following.

score.justification_pass1: The teacher repeats the same analogy without addressing the student's explicit confusion about where b starts from, and the student shows no progress in understanding that arrows represent movements from their starting positions rather than from zero.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher consistently uses concrete real-world analogies (driving on a road, walking on a playground) to represent abstract number line operations, which is a strong implementation of the experiential strategy, though the repetition in Turn 3 suggests some limitation in adapting the approach.
